This is the answer. It's the same as any other art that is just treated as 'entertainment media'. Movies are plagued by this, music is plagued by this.
The sad thing is that consumers are accepting of big companies reusing the same template over and over and still buy the shit
This is highly related to the studio producing the game, not the one developing it.
Because the devs have learned that they can feed us anything and we'll eat it all up. Case in point: sports games.
I still can't get over that... Sports games!

As someone who thoroughly enjoys sports game, I'm pretty sure most people don't buy the game every year. I go by a policy where I won't buy a new one until they add a significant feature or 3-4 years have passed.

Consumers won't stand up to corporations anymore, and they continue to be enticed into pre-ordering and blindly purchasing. Boycotts and negative reviews just don't happen anymore. The corporations know they'll get their money one way or the other.

The developers are who we hear from early on. They are the ones hyping up the game, then the production company pushes it out the door before its finished. Wildstar, Batman: Arkham Knight, Sim City, Hellgate London. All these games had great potential and were killed by an early release due to publisher pressure

I feel like as games get more and more complicated, especially graphically, glitches are bound to happen and in some cases unavoidable. Even the absolute best, most polished and finished games ever have plenty of glitches. It seems as if they are more prevalent because people really like to point them out on gaming sites and blame it on laziness, which could also be the case.

Because of publishers in my opinion. The put stress on the developers, thus creating a rushed game. Its like trying to get a musician to write a symphony in three hours. People will come and listen if the name is big enough, but the piece will be terrible. Unless you are Beethoven that is.
I pre order and get every piece of dlc for every game and each one runs absolutely perfect

The complexity of big high end graphic games has improved a lot and the development is a lot harder then it was in the past, organisation also does not get easier as the product gets bigger.

It is not only the fault of greedy publishers or incompetent devs alone. It might be a factor in it, but I can't believe that anyone would not prefer to release a bug free game. Just makes no sense to me.

Aside from apathy, AAA titles rely on large groups of peoples and importantly, programmers. Getting a number of people all writing code on different parts and with different mentalities can result in a lot of issues and bugs.

Because AAA games from large publishers are about marketing more than about actual quality. Your game will sell well if the people buying it are clueless parents in supermarkets. You can dance on your head over the internet, you will never make these people informed. You yourself are also clueless about countless things you buy.

Because programmers are criminally inept at estimating how much time it will take them to do something, and marketing won't take "We need more time to finish this" as an excuse unless the developers have some form of legitimate time frame to give them.

It's why more and more companies that employ software engineers require them to use very rigid development processes. A well-built process will be extremely front-loaded, with more than 50% of the 'work' being completed before they even open up an IDE, and then a ton of post-completion collection of statistics. If a programmer has data from past projects that they can look at and say "Hm, well, over my last 500,000 lines of code, I know that I generally complete about X lines of code per hour, and inject Y amount of bugs her 1000 lines", so assuming I work at a similar pace... blahblahblah. It also lets them go back and analyze similar things they've done in the past, and so get a rough estimate of how many lines of code they think some particular module will take. It's much easier to go to marketing and say "Looking at my team's past performance, it will take us Z days to finish these specific parts" instead of "Yeah, we're not done. Give us more time, please."

Like, if you were building a bridge, would you just throw one together and then drive some cars over it to see if it works? No. You make totally fucking sure that it's going to work before you even break ground. Software is trying to shift in this direction, but decades of bad practice is a hard thing to erase.

Also the advent of patching has led publishers into thinking "We need to release this now. If it doesn't work 100%, we can just patch it." Back in the cartridge/disc era, if your game wasn't done, you couldn't release it.
